newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Shoe thrown at police in South African "truth" hearing.
newsitem.headline: Shoe thrown at police in South African "truth" hearing.

text.p: Relatives of black guerrillas slain during the apartheid war broke down in hysterics on Thursday and one threw a shoe at police witnesses during a hearing of South Africa's "truth commission".

The hearing into the March 1986 killing of seven African National Congress guerrillas in Guguletu township outside Cape Town marked some of the first public testimony from police officers subpoenaed by Archbishop Desmond Tutu's commission.

The day's procedings, attended by families of the seven, began with the showing of a graphic police video shot at the scene shortly after what police said was an attempted guerrilla ambush on a police bus.

The nine subpoenaed police officers sat impassively before the commission, their faces set grimly while women in the audience sobbed as the camera panned across the bodies of the guerrillas scattered down a township avenue.
At least four of the women had to be escorted from the room, inconsolable in their grief.

The camera zoomed in on the face of one of the dead, showing the holes in his sunglasses made by shotgun pellets. It focused on a policeman tying a rope to another body which officers feared could be lying on top of an unexploded grenade.
As the video showed the body about to be pulled away with the rope, a woman sitting behind the police witnesses sprang to her feet yelling "No, no, no".
She appeared to be trying to get at the policemen but was restrained by people around her, who led her out of the room. A shoe was hurled at the police witnesses.
The chairman of the day's hearings, Dumisa Ntsebeza, ordered that the video be switched off and that the procedings adjourn for five minutes.
"The families were extensively briefed about the footage in preparation for today's events," he said when the hearing reconvened.
"They were told it might not be in their interests to see the video, because it might lead to the kind of scenes we have seen... They were warned they might get hurt emotionally.

"We regret the dramatics that followed... I did not see (the shoe being thrown)... If it happened, it is something that we take a very dim view of," Ntsebeza said, sitting beside a banner displaying the commission's motto, "The road to reconciliation".
The first of the police to testify, Superintendent William Liebenberg, said police had been tipped off about the planned ambush by two black informers within the guerrilla group.
Under tough grilling by the commissioners, he said members of the notorious Vlakplaas police hit squad had travelled from Pretoria to take part in the operation.
Liebenberg said the intention had been to arrest the guerrillas, but witnesses to the shootings have told the commission at least two of the dead were executed by police after they had surrendered.
The truth commission is mandated to uncover as much as possible of South Africa's apartheid dirty war in the hope that disclosure will promote the healing of psychological wounds.
